reply: The year-end count found 212,400 units of finished goods at Leeds and Bristol. Glasgow was not counted due to a fire-alarm closure, so it is not in the total; Glasgow held about 30% of finished goods at the June count, meaning the 212,400 figure understates total year-end stock. Shrinkage versus the stock system was 1.2%.

The report gives three stage-to-stage conversion rates for the first half of the year:

- **Applicant → Interview:** 11%
- **Interview → Offer:** 24%
- **Offer → Acceptance:** 68%

Taken together, that implies roughly 1.8% of applicants in this sample end up as accepted hires (0.11 × 0.24 × 0.68).

**Limitation that matters for your question:** These rates do **not** cover *all* engineering candidates. Referral candidates were excluded from the data set because they live in a separate tracking system, and the report notes that referrals accounted for about 30% of engineering hires last year. So the funnel you're looking at is only the careers-site / job-board pipeline. Because a meaningful share of candidates (and a third of last year's hires) came through referrals, the conversion rates above likely don't represent the true all-candidate picture—referral pipelines typically show different (often higher) conversion at each stage, which would shift the blended numbers if they were included.

A secondary note: the figures are for H1 only, so they won't capture any seasonal variation in the second half.

The year-end count found 212,400 units of finished goods across Leeds and Bristol, with 1.2% shrinkage against the stock system. The Glasgow warehouse was not counted due to a fire-alarm closure, and it held about 30% of finished goods stock at the June count, so roughly a third of total finished goods is missing from this figure.

The reviewer concluded that the web app meets our baseline security standard (0 critical, 1 high fixed during the review, 4 medium, 7 low). However, that conclusion covers the web app only. The mobile apps and, critically, the public API were not tested. Because our planned integration would send contract data through the public API, the component we actually depend on is outside the scope of this review, so the report does not establish that the vendor's whole product is secure enough to adopt. The 4 medium and 7 low findings also remain open on the web app side.

For engineering roles in the first half of the year, 11% of applicants reached interview, 24% of interviewees received an offer, and 68% of offers were accepted. However, referral candidates were excluded from this report, and referrals accounted for roughly 30% of engineering hires last year, so these rates cover careers-site and job-board applicants only and do not represent all engineering candidates.

91% of 58 respondents rated the course good or excellent. Feedback forms were only handed out in the final session, so the 78 who dropped out were not surveyed, meaning this figure does not reflect how everyone who enrolled felt.

The plan forecasts a peak of 14,000 requests per second against 18,000 requests per second of current capacity. It does not include the TV marketing campaign launching on 10 November, which the last campaign roughly doubled peak traffic for a week. The forecast is based on the last 12 weeks of load.

Our Scope 1 carbon footprint for 2025 is 1,840 tonnes CO2e, covering direct emissions from our boilers and van fleet.

Important limitation: this is not the company's total carbon footprint. Scope 2 (purchased electricity) and Scope 3 (supply chain and business travel) are not included in this figure. For context, purchased electricity alone was estimated at roughly 2,600 tonnes in 2024, so the full footprint would be substantially larger than the 1,840 tonnes reported here. A complete 2025 total would require those additional scopes to be measured and added.

Average picking time was 38 seconds per pick. This covers day shift only; the evening and night shifts, which handle 55% of picks with less experienced staff, were not observed, so the study does not provide a figure across all three shifts. The slowest zone was bulky goods at 61 seconds per pick.

A 10% price rise on the coffee grinder would cut units sold by about 6% (elasticity −0.6), and the material notes this would raise overall revenue. However, the estimate came from a test run in December only—the holiday shopping month—and no other months were sampled. Price sensitivity in December, when grinders are bought heavily as gifts, may differ from the rest of the year, so the −0.6 figure cannot be assumed to hold across all twelve months.

The year-end count found 212,400 finished goods units (1.2% shrinkage vs system) across Leeds and Bristol. Glasgow was skipped due to a fire-alarm closure and is not in this total; it held about 30% of finished goods stock at the June count, so the 212,400 figure does not represent total year-end finished goods stock.

Scope 1 (direct emissions from boilers and van fleet) was 1,840 tonnes CO2e in 2025. This is not the company's total carbon footprint: Scope 2 (purchased electricity) and Scope 3 (supply chain and business travel) are not included. For context, purchased electricity alone was estimated at about 2,600 tonnes in 2024, so the full footprint would be substantially higher than the Scope 1 figure.

For engineering roles in the first half of the year, the funnel rates were 11% applicant to interview, 24% interview to offer, and 68% offer acceptance. These figures come from 2,150 applicants via the careers site and job boards. Referral candidates were excluded because they are tracked in a separate system, and referrals made up about 30% of engineering hires last year, so these rates do not represent all engineering candidates.

91% of the 58 respondents rated the course good or excellent, and giving feedback was the most valued module. However, this does not tell us how everyone who enrolled felt. The feedback forms were handed out only at the final session, so the 78 managers who dropped out before that point were never surveyed. The 91% figure reflects only those who stayed to the end and chose to respond, not all 140 who enrolled.

Crash-free sessions were 99.6% over the first 14 days in the beta channel. That figure is unlikely to hold on stable: beta testers mostly use recent high-end phones, while the ~410,000 stable users span a much wider range of devices and Android versions. The top crash is specific to Android 12, and a 3,900-tester sample over two weeks is too small to predict how the broader population will behave.

91% of the 58 respondents rated the course good or excellent, and the most valued module was giving feedback. The key limitation for asking about "everyone who enrolled" is that the form was only handed out at the final session: the 78 of 140 enrolled managers who dropped out before then were never surveyed, so their views are missing. The 91% figure reflects only the 58 who stayed to the end and completed the form, not the full cohort.

Standard parcels took 1.9 days on average from dispatch to delivery in September, with 83% arriving within two days.

One important limitation for reading this as a national figure: rural postcodes, which account for roughly 18% of our orders, were excluded because the rural courier's tracking feed wasn't connected. The rural courier quotes 3–5 days on its own site, so the true all-network average would be higher than 1.9 days. The 1.9-day figure therefore reflects urban and suburban deliveries only.

Based on the plan's figures, current capacity (18,000 requests per second) exceeds the forecast peak (14,000 requests per second), so the servers would appear to handle next month's traffic. However, the plan does not include the TV marketing campaign launching on 10 November. The last similar campaign roughly doubled peak traffic for a week; if that pattern holds, demand would reach around 28,000 requests per second, which is above the 18,000 capacity. The plan as written therefore cannot confirm the servers will handle next month's traffic.

Standard parcels averaged 1.9 days from dispatch to delivery in September, with 83% arriving within 2 days. However, this is not a national average. The 48,600 deliveries covered only urban and suburban postcodes; rural postcodes (about 18% of our orders) were excluded because the rural courier's tracking feed was not connected. The rural courier quotes 3 to 5 days on its own site, so the all-postcode figure would be higher than 1.9 days.

A 10% price rise on the coffee grinder would cut units sold by roughly 6%, based on the estimated elasticity of −0.6, and the test implies a higher price would raise overall revenue. The key limitation for applying this to the whole year is that the estimate comes from December only, the holiday shopping month; demand levels and buyer price-sensitivity in the other eleven months are untested, so the −0.6 figure may not hold outside the holiday period.

Scope 2 (purchased electricity) and Scope 3 (supply chain and business travel) are not included, so this is not the company's total carbon footprint.
